cue: The sharpest part is a band along the waterline.
rows: Crocodiles see most sharply along a band level with the horizon. It lets them scan the waterline without turning their heads.
Crocodiles have three kinds of colour-sensing cells, as people do, so this view leaves colours as your camera shows them.
An alligator’s pupil is a vertical slit. It smears out-of-focus things up and down, and this view does the same.
Field of view, sharpness, dim light and depth
These parts of the view are guesses.

rows: A level band of sharper sight

Juvenile saltwater crocodiles resolve about 8.8 cycles per degree and juvenile freshwater crocodiles 8.0, counted from the densest nerve cells in a horizontal streak across the retina. No count was found for an alligator itself, so this picture sits halfway between them, far coarser than the 30 a human reads on a chart.

Crocodile retinas carry a horizontal streak with about four times the cell density of the periphery. Nobody has measured how fast your sharpness falls away above and below it, so the softness of the edges is a guess.

A juvenile saltwater crocodile has three single cones that peak near 424, 502 and 546 nanometers, and a freshwater crocodile near 426, 510 and 554. An American alligator has four cone pigments, at 444 and 535 in single cones and at 566 and 503 in the double cone, so you very likely see color across the violet, green and red ends of the spectrum.

Your retina is mostly rods, with one rod pigment that peaks near 501 nanometers, and a layer of crystals behind the retina bounces light back through it. A spectacled caiman is said to see in both day and night.
A juvenile saltwater crocodile has a mobile slit for a pupil. The record says nothing about which way the slit runs.
An American alligator hears from 100 hertz to 8 kilohertz in air, best near 1000 hertz, and from 100 hertz to 2 kilohertz in water, best near 800 hertz. Sound reaches you with no picture of its own.

Nobody has measured which way your pupil slit runs, how bright the glow behind your retina looks to another animal, at what light level your colors turn to rod colors, or how your cone signals blend into the colors you experience.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: Two of your relatives, the saltwater crocodile and the freshwater crocodile, have a streak of sharpest vision that runs across the back of each eye from the nose side to the temple side. At its best the saltwater crocodile sees about 9 cycles a degree, less than a third of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured where your sharpest spot lies or how sharply you see.
rows.note: Records cover only Crocodylus species; nothing for Alligator, so the row stays at i.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are an American alligator, the cone cells in your eyes hold four kinds of light-sensing pigment, where a human has three. One of them sits in a single cone and senses light most strongly at 535 nanometers. If you are a saltwater crocodile, your three kinds of single cone sense violet, green and red light most strongly.
rows.note: Only one of the alligator's four pigment peaks is recorded (535 nm), so the others are left out. Caimans and most crocodiles are not covered by this row.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are an American alligator, the dark opening in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a China alligator, you very likely have the same, since your close relative the American alligator does. Among crocodiles, the saltwater crocodile has a vertical, mobile slit pupil, and nobody has measured the pupil shape of the other crocodiles, the caimans or the gharial.
rows.note: Removed the word "report". Caiman, gharial and most crocodile species have no pupil record, so the row says nobody has measured them.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness, dim light and depth
rows.text: Nobody has measured how wide you see, how sharply you see, how little light you need or how you judge distance. Crocodilians have a reflecting layer in the eye that helps them see at night, and you very likely have one as well. In six crocodilian species, the eyes focused well on distant things in air and were badly out of focus underwater.
rows.note: The saltwater crocodile's sharpness figure is left to the Sharpest spot row, and the reflecting layer is described without the furrowed slit. No record measures the American alligator for these traits.
rows.rewrite_reason: Draft repeats the 9 cycles from Sharpest spot, and 'brightest behind a furrowed slit' reads like the pupil. Cut both; live says nothing.
